intent: Treat performance as a stated requirement with a budget, measured before it is changed — and spend optimisation effort only where a measurement says the cost is.
problem: Performance is either ignored until it becomes an incident, or 'optimised' from intuition, which reliably targets the wrong code. The first failure produces a rewrite; the second produces obfuscated code, an unreproducible slowdown, and a codebase nobody dares touch because the optimisation's rationale is undocumented.
context: The governing evidence is Knuth's 1974 line that programmers waste enormous time worrying about the speed of non-critical parts, combined with his follow-up that in the 1971 empirical study of Fortran programs under 4% of a program accounted for about half its running time. The balance is not 'performance doesn't matter': it is that algorithm and data-structure choices are big efficiencies and belong at design time, while micro-tunings are small efficiencies and belong after measurement. Amdahl's law caps the return on optimising any part, so a measured profile decides where effort goes.
benefits: Optimisation effort goes where the profile says time is spent, not where intuition guessed.
Correctness is not sacrificed to speed: correctness first, then measurement, then change.
The cost of the change is justified by a number, so the decision survives code review.
A performance budget makes a regression visible before it becomes an incident.
Big wins are captured at design time by choosing the right algorithm and data structure.
tradeoffs: Requiring a measurement before every performance change adds friction and demands profiling skills.
Performance budgets and representative load data are themselves a maintenance burden.
Amdahl-bound optimisations can plateau; past that point only a redesign or more hardware helps.
Optimised code is usually less readable, and readability regressions persist long after the traffic spike does.
Profiling environments differ from production, so the measurement can point at the wrong bottleneck.
quality_attributes_note: performance 10 and scalability 9 are the point. maintainability 5 reflects the real cost: performance-motivated code is harder to read. observability 9 because a profile you cannot trust is worse than none.

participants.responsibility: A stated budget or target (latency percentile, throughput, memory, payload) that makes performance a testable property.
participants.notes: Without a number, "fast enough" is unfalsifiable and the argument is settled by seniority.

participants.responsibility: A profile, benchmark or load test on representative data; the gate on any speed-motivated change.
participants.notes: Knuth: a priori judgements about which parts are critical are usually wrong.

participants.responsibility: The small fraction of code that dominates runtime.
participants.notes: Under 4% of a program accounted for about half its running time in Knuth's 1971 study.

use_cases: Choosing an index or a data structure from a measured query profile before writing the code.
Rejecting a pull request that hand-unrolls a loop with no profile attached.
Setting a p99 latency budget for an endpoint and asserting it in a load test.
Replacing an O(n^2) scan with a hash lookup because a profile showed it, not because it looked slow.
Adding a cache after measuring that the upstream call dominates, rather than speculatively.
avoid_when: The code runs once in a script and the cost is irrelevant.
The measurement environment does not resemble production, so any conclusion is unfounded.
The change is a large-constant-factor algorithm or data-structure improvement at design time — that is a design decision, not micro-optimisation, and needs no profile of existing code.
The bottleneck is a known physical limit (network round-trip, disk seek) that code cannot remove.
pitfalls: Using "premature optimization is the root of all evil" to shut down legitimate design-time performance discussion.
Optimising from intuition, which is unreliable even for experienced programmers.
Unrolling loops, caching fields and adding manual buffer management with no profile attached.
Benchmarking a micro-operation in a loop that the optimiser can eliminate or hoist.
Optimising the average when the product requirement is a tail percentile.
Measured-and-true complexity: code so contorted that the next change is riskier than the speedup was worth.

related_patterns_notes.data-locality: The structural cause of most real slowdowns: memory access costs, not instruction counts. A profile usually points here first.
related_patterns_notes.memoization: Cache-before-measure is the speculative form; apply it once a profile shows the recomputation.
related_patterns_notes.cache-aside: The canonical caching pattern, which should be reached for on evidence rather than by default.
related_patterns_notes.backpressure: A throughput concern handled at design time — the efficiency that Knuth's 'critical 3%' actually covers.

anti_patterns: Micro-optimisation applied uniformly because someone quoted Knuth out of context.
Benchmarking an unrepresentative dataset and making a design decision from it.
Caching every method call "for performance" with no invalidation strategy.
Obfuscated code whose only defence is "it needs to be fast".
Optimising the hot path while the dominant cost is a network round-trip per item.
design_principles: We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3% (Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements, 1974).

It is often a mistake to make a priori judgments about what parts of a program are really critical, since the universal experience of programmers who have been using measurement tools has been that their intuitive guesses fail (Knuth 1974).
Less than 4% of a program generally accounts for about half of its running time (Knuth, An Empirical Study of Fortran Programs, 1971).
More computing sins are committed in the name of efficiency than for any other single reason, including blind stupidity (W. A. Wulf).
Amdahl's law caps the achievable speed-up by the fraction of time the optimised part consumes.
Latency is a distribution; the average hides the tail where the slowest users live.
best_practices: Write the budget down first: a percentile latency target, throughput, or memory ceiling, so "fast" is falsifiable.
Require a profile or benchmark before merging any change justified by speed; reject it if the number did not move.
Pick the algorithm and the data structure first — no amount of tuning changes the complexity class.
Profile with representative data and watch percentiles, not means.
Let the compiler optimise the uninteresting 97%; reserve manual effort for what it cannot do.
Benchmark hot code so an optimisation is not silently deleted by a later refactor.
